name: PT Bank Pan Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Panin Bank — a deposit franchise that does not earn its cost of capital
frontmatter.summary: Panin Bank trades at a steep discount to book, but its return on equity sits far below the cost of equity and the loan book is shrinking in a market growing at double digits. The discount is not a mispricing we can close: fair value is below the market price even after a peer-consistent risk premium and one consistent terminal return. REDUCE, with the dividend the only support and surplus capital the main upside risk.
thesis: Panin earns a return on equity of roughly half its cost of equity; a bank in that position is worth less than its book, not more, and the residual-income and warranted P/BV methods agree.
The discount to book is real but not wide enough. The market already prices about a third of book; our warranted multiple is below that, so the cheapness is optical rather than investable.
Loans grew no faster than the deposit base while the industry compounded double digits, so Panin is ceding share deliberately; that protects credit quality but caps the earnings base.

The margin improvement of 2026 is a funding-mix swap, with cheap deposits up and time deposits down; the regulator projects the industry margin stable rather than falling, so we carry a modest ten-basis-point improvement path from a CASA base well below the large franchises, not a collapse.

A payout near two-fifths of earnings funds a dividend yield that is the return anchor, and a capital ratio above thirty percent means no dilution risk — but it also means a capital-return prize over a third of the equity base that no board has committed to; both tails model the board returning about half of earnings, and the base case keeps the declared payout and does not pay for it.

blocks.text: **Rating REDUCE, target Rp509 against a price of Rp725, a total return of -24.0% including the dividend.** Panin Bank is a family-controlled, sub-scale Indonesian commercial bank that lends at a margin slightly above the industry and earned a return on equity of 5.1% in the last financial year against a cost of equity of 12.5% [S0][S5]. The shares change hands at 0.3x times book, and the question for an owner is whether that discount compensates for a franchise that does not cover its cost of capital. Our answer is that it does not: warranted P/BV at the three-year sustainable return of 5.0% is 0.2x times, below the traded multiple, and the largest-weighted residual-income model puts a similar value on the equity [S0].

The variant view is not that Panin is a bad bank — it is conservatively run, over-capitalised at a capital adequacy ratio of 36.6%, and it has improved its funding mix and its gross NPL ratio this year [S5]. The variant view is that the market's discount already credits the bank with a partial recovery that the numbers do not support. The loan book is flat in a market compounding at 13.7% [S5][S7], the margin gain came from swapping time deposits for current accounts rather than from pricing power [S5], and the provisions line is still rising faster than the book [S3]. Growth is therefore neither credit-fuelled nor capital-constrained: it is absent, and the return on equity that follows from it stays near 4.9% [S0].

What moves the value, in order: the credit-cost path through the remaining impaired book, the durability of the 4.3% margin against a falling industry margin, and any capital action forced by the free-float rule [S6][S8]. The dividend of Rp42 per share, a yield of 5.7%, is the return anchor and the floor under the shares [S0]. The bull case needs a lower credit cost and a return to growth; the bear case needs the loan book to keep shrinking and provisioning to keep climbing [S3][S4].

Panin Bank is a commercial bank with a multi-finance subsidiary, operating through banking and multi-finance segments and offering savings, deposits, consumer and business credit, treasury and sharia products through a branch network and, since 2026, the MyPanin application [S0][S3]. The franchise is corporate- and SME-weighted with a consumer mortgage book; the bank describes its lending as selective and risk-led rather than volume-led [S3]. Its funding base is customer deposits of IDR156,920.0bn, of which the cheap current-and-savings component is 40.9% [S5]. It also funds itself in the bond market, issuing IDR3,200.0bn of senior bonds in 2025 across three tranches of a rolling programme [S4].

Revenue is dominated by the spread on the loan book: net interest income of IDR8,631.6bn against non-interest income of IDR1,768.6bn [S0]. Within the loan book the corporate and commercial segments carry the larger balances at thinner spreads, while the consumer and mortgage book carries the higher yield and, historically, the higher loss experience; the multi-finance subsidiary adds consumer instalment lending on top [S0][S3]. That mix matters for the forecast: the bank can defend the margin by lending to corporates, but it cannot lift the return on equity that way, because the same mix that keeps credit cost contained also keeps the spread narrow.

The scale is the point. Gross loans of IDR145,080.0bn make Panin a mid-tier lender, and the book shrank in FY2025 [S4], then broadly flat over the following nine months [S5]. Management is explicit that the shrinkage is a choice: credit is "dikendalikan secara prudent" because demand is limited and rates are high [S3]. In a system whose loan book grew 13.7%, Panin is not a challenger taking share; it is a lender managing a runoff of the segments where its impaired loans sit [S7].

Control is concentrated. The founding Gunawan family's vehicle, Panin Financial, and the ANZ-linked Votraint entity have been joint controllers since the regulator formalised the arrangement, and the listed shares in public hands are 11.9% of the total [S0]. The two controlling blocks are named in the company's shareholding register rather than in the market-data record we can reach, so we state the aggregate float and do not split the remainder between the vehicles; the consequences of that structure — liquidity, index treatment, and the free-float rule — are set out in section six [S6]. We could not archive a related-party disclosure deep enough to size the family's other ventures' access to the balance sheet (section six).

The Indonesian banking system is large, growing and increasingly concentrated. System loans grew 13.7% at August 2026, the fastest in a decade, while system deposits grew 10.9% [S7]. The policy rate has been held unchanged since the October meeting [S7], and the industry net interest margin has been compressing: 4.3% in August 2026 against a materially higher level a year earlier, which the regulator attributes to the policy rate, cost of funds, loan mix and risk profiles, and which the same regulator projects forward at a stable and moderate level on effective transmission [S8]. That is the sector backdrop against which Panin's own margin of 4.4% should be read — Panin is slightly above the industry, and the forward path is neither a collapse nor an extension [S5][S8].

Regulation shapes the competitive map in two ways. Capital and liquidity buffers are ample across the system, so the constraint on lending is demand rather than capital [S7]. And the listing rule requiring a minimum free float now covers a group of banks that sit below it, with the regulator offering rights issues and mergers as routes to compliance and flexibility by ownership structure and capital need [S6]. Panin, at 11.9% free float, is below that threshold [S0]; the article does not name it, so the exposure is our inference from the float rather than a company statement [S6]. That makes a corporate action a live structural question for the shares — a placement or rights issue changes the supply — without making it dated.

The macro deck's caution on rate-sensitive Indonesian financials is the external influence that matters here, and it is worth being precise about why it bites this name and not the rest of the covered sector [S0]. The tilt is sector-wide: with the currency under pressure and the policy rate held, the sector's funding cost is sticky while its loan yield is not, and the regulator's own data show the industry margin already falling [S8]. The five peers rated BUY on the same deck are not exempt from that; they absorb it because they fund themselves more cheaply, run far lower cost-to-income and earn a return above their cost of equity, so a modest industry margin squeeze is a slice of excess return rather than the whole margin of safety. Here it lands differently: the cheap-deposit share is 40.9%, well below the large franchises; the loan book is flat while the system grows 13.7% [S5][S7]; and the return on equity is already below the cost of equity. The same sector-wide move therefore takes the return further from the cost of capital instead of trimming a surplus. The deck is the backdrop, not the reason for the rating: the call differs from the peers because of the company evidence, and it would survive the deck being wrong.

Competitively, Panin is a price-taker in a market where the moat belongs to the large deposit franchises: the big banks fund themselves more cheaply, lend at scale and take the fee pools. The system's own growth arithmetic shows why the gap widens — loan growth is outrunning deposit growth, so every bank is competing for the same rupiah of funding, and the banks with the cheapest current-account franchises win that contest without paying for it [S7]. Panin's answer has been to shrink the loan book rather than bid for deposits, which protects the margin and the capital ratio but leaves it further behind each year. Panin's own advantage is narrow — a long-standing corporate relationships book, a recognisable consumer brand, and a capital ratio that lets it absorb losses rather than chase volume [S5]. Against the five forces: supplier power among depositors is high and rising as time-deposit competition returns; buyer power is high for corporate borrowers; the threat of new entrants is real in digital banking but not in the segments Panin serves; substitutes are fintech lending at the margin; and rivalry is intensifying because system loan growth is running ahead of deposit growth [S7][S8]. On that map Panin is a disciplined but structurally sub-scale participant, and its positioning explains both the low return on equity and the absence of a credible path to a high one.

The historical record is one of a bank shrinking slowly and earning a low return on a large equity base. Net interest income was IDR8,631.6bn in FY2025 on a book of IDR145,080.0bn, with non-interest income of IDR1,768.6bn; net profit to parent was IDR2,750.0bn and the return on equity 5.1% [S0]. One labelling point on that history: the net interest income line is the data pack's, and the company reports that net interest income grew by a fifth of one per cent for FY2025 [S4], which on the pack's FY2024A base implies a level slightly below the modelled one — a pack-versus-filing difference of under two per cent, disclosed here and with no forecast effect, because forward net interest income is built from earning assets and margin rather than grown off the line [S0][S4]. The reported fee line grew to IDR2,300.0bn, but the company attributes the increase mainly to gains on securities transactions rather than recurring fees [S4] — which is why we forecast the non-interest line at a modest growth rate and do not capitalise it as a franchise.

On our forecasts the loan book grows marginally in FY2026E to IDR145,805.4bn, the run-rate the nine-month prints imply, then at a mid-single-digit rate as capital is retained and the impaired stock is worked down [S4][S5]. Deposits grow slightly faster to keep the loan-to-deposit ratio near the 90.1% the bank actually prints [S5]. The margin carries a modest improvement from the nine-month level, 4.3%, to 4.5%, because the funding-mix swap still has room — CASA at 40.9% is well below the large franchises — and the regulator projects the industry margin forward as stable rather than falling [S5][S8]. Cost-to-income is set at 50.0%, the level the one quarter with both lines filed implies: pre-provision profit of IDR1,290.0bn on the quarter's own operating income line [S3][S0], which cross-checks because that pre-provision line less the reported provision of IDR350.7bn reproduces the quarter's pre-tax profit [S3][S0]. We must be explicit that this is the only period we can verify. Neither the FY2025 nor the nine-month results article states an opex, provision or BOPO figure, and no company financial statement could be archived — the IR site refuses our fetcher and IDX is out of scope by design — so the FY2025 split between cost and provisioning is unverified and we have not closed it with a residual number [S4][S5]. The cost base is therefore an assumption, not an observation, and it is one-sided: if FY2025 provisioning had run at the prior-year quarterly rate annualised, cost-to-income would have been well above our number and the target materially lower, which is the direction of the bear case. Credit cost is set at 0.9%, above the reported run-rate because a gross NPL ratio of 3.0% and a net NPL ratio still above one percent say the book is still impaired [S3][S5]; restructured, special-mention and stage-two balances, and the NPL coverage ratio, are not disclosed in any source we could archive, so the through-cycle rate is a judgement with that gap stated rather than a calibrated output [S4][S5]. The result is a return on equity that drifts from 4.9% to 5.4% — an improvement, but one that never approaches the cost of equity [S0].

Earnings quality, per the financials screen. The relevant test for a bank is the provisioning-versus-write-off trend, not the accruals ratio. Here the gross NPL ratio improved to 2.8% in FY2025 and 3.0% in September 2026, but provisions rose by a third year on year in the first quarter of 2026 to IDR350.7bn [S3][S4][S5] — the pattern of write-offs keeping the headline clean while real credit cost climbs. That is an optics-class flag: we model the cash cost, not the ratio, and we do not credit the improvement in gross NPL as an earnings source. Two further optics-class items: the bank revalues premises under the fixed-asset revaluation rules, which inflates book value relative to a historical-cost basis and argues for caution on any P/BV floor; and the disclosure on related-party lending is not deep enough in the public record to quantify, which we flag rather than assume away. No manipulation-class flag was found in what we could examine: the reported numbers are internally consistent across three periods, and there is no evidence of fabrication or serial dilution in the record [S3][S4][S5]. The governance gate itself is only partly verified, and we say so in section six rather than present it as cleared.

The balance sheet is liquid to the point of inefficiency. Total assets of IDR237,326.7bn against loans of IDR145,080.0bn and deposits of IDR156,920.0bn leave a large securities and placement book earning a thinner spread than the loan book, which is why the reported margin sits below the loan yield [S0][S5]. A bank holding that much liquidity through a cycle is safe and unexciting; it also means a return to lending would lift the margin without any pricing decision, which is the upside the bull case is really about.

Capital allocation is simple and, given the returns, correct: pay out 37.0% of earnings and retain the rest against a capital ratio of 36.6% that is far above any regulatory need [S5]. Book value per share compounds from Rp2,284 to Rp2,698 over the forecast, entirely from retained earnings; there is no buyback, no acquisition and no dilution in the base case. Debt is the bond programme described above plus the subordinated tier-two issue, and it is comfortably serviced by a balance sheet of this quality [S4].

Banks are valued on equity, not enterprise value, so the method set is the banks card's: residual income carries the largest weight in this note, while warranted P/BV — the engine's configured primary lens for the industry — and a dividend discount are the cross-checks. The cost of equity is built, not asserted, and the build is disclosed in full: a risk-free rate of 7.4% on the long rupiah curve less the sovereign default spread of 1.6% the engine applies to strip the credit component out of the government yield, plus a levered beta of 0.9x on an equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, plus a company-specific premium of 0.6%; the result is 12.5% [KB macro deck, 2026; house config]. The rates, beta and premium are the house inputs, not company data. The premium is the piece the first version of this note left out, and it is not decorative: the three published Indonesian bank peers in our own coverage carry between sixty and ninety-five basis points on the same engine build, so a sub-scale bank with a three-percent NPL ratio and a free float near one in nine cannot be priced sixty basis points inside the best-in-class franchise. Sixty basis points is the bottom of the peer range, so the cost of equity used here is the generous end. Enterprise-level gearing is set to zero because a bank is valued on the equity side [KB macro deck, 2026; house config].

The largest-weighted residual-income model discounts the excess of net profit over the cost of equity on opening book, with a terminal growth of 3.2%. That growth is not the deck's nominal path. The banks card caps growth at the retention-funded rate, the return on equity times one minus the payout, and a single growth rate has to sit inside every lens that uses it: the residual-income terminal is driven by the model's FY2035E return of 5.5%, whose own cap is higher, while the warranted P/BV cross-check applies the engine's three-year-average sustainable return of 5.0%, whose cap is the binding one. Growth is set at that lower cap, so no lens grows book faster than the return it earns can fund, and the two methods are no longer fed different terminal economics [S0]. The residual-income model returns Rp398 per share and warranted P/BV 0.2x times book, or Rp452 [S0]. The dividend discount model returns Rp526, 16.5% above the engine's primary warranted-P/BV lens — the divergence the engine flags, and it is explained by the model's assumption that a rising dividend stream can be capitalised at the same growth rate regardless of the earnings that fund it; for a bank that retains more than half its profit at a return below its cost of equity, that is too generous, so the DDM carries the smallest weight.

At Rp725 the shares trade at 0.3x times our FY2026E book and 6.4x times earnings, with a dividend yield of 5.7% [S0]. Reverse-engineering the price against the warranted-P/BV lens, the multiple the market pays requires an implied credit cost of 0.2% — roughly a fifth of our through-cycle charge and below any rate the bank has printed — so the price embeds a recovery in asset quality the franchise has not shown [S0][S5]. The gap between the traded multiple and the warranted multiple is the whole thesis. Surplus capital is real and large: on a twenty-percent capital-adequacy target about IDR24,650.0bn of the capital stack sits above the need, around Rp1,024 per share [S5][S0]. That figure is not by itself a per-share value — it is capital inside the balance sheet, and at a return below the cost of equity every rupiah of it retained is a drag — so what it is worth depends on the distribution path, and both tails model one rather than naming it. Both scenario tails lift the payout to about half of earnings: the bull because returns improve, the bear because a shrinking book needs less capital and retaining it at a return below the cost of equity destroys value. That lifts the bull value to Rp831, above the Rp725 price, and the post-distribution return on equity rises because the same earnings run on a smaller equity base [S0]. A one-off special dividend or buyback of the whole surplus is neither declared nor dated, so it is not modelled separately; the higher payout is the permanent, board-decidable version of the same channel, and the free-float remedy is the mechanism that could force the board's hand (section six). The base case keeps the declared payout, because no increase has been announced, so the base does not pay for the capital return and the tails test it.

The downside risks, with likelihood and impact. **Credit (high likelihood, high impact):** a gross NPL ratio of 3.0% and a net NPL ratio above one percent on a book that has been shrinking means the impaired stock is not being grown away; a slower workout keeps credit cost at or above our 0.9% assumption [S5]. **Macro and rates (medium, medium):** the policy rate has been held unchanged with the currency under pressure, and the sector deck is cautious on rate-sensitive Indonesian banks; that caution is sector-wide, and as section two sets out it takes the return away from the cost of capital here — rather than trimming a surplus — because the deposit franchise is thin at a CASA ratio of 40.9% and the book is flat [S7][S8][S0]. **Regulatory and structural (medium, medium):** the free-float rule requires a minimum holding in public hands and Panin sits below it; the remedy is a placement or rights issue, which changes the share supply and could price at a discount [S6][S0]. **Liquidity (medium, medium):** the free float is 11.9% of the shares and turnover is thin relative to the float, so an owner cannot assume an exit at the screen price; the model applies no liquidity discount because the house has no discount table for this and we would rather show the gap than bury it, which means the target should be read as an upper bound for a size-constrained buyer. **Governance and related parties (medium, high impact, unquantified):** joint control by the founding family and a legacy foreign shareholder has produced a bank run for stability rather than value, and the related-party disclosure in the record we could reach is too thin to size the family's other ventures' exposure; because an impairment of book value is the one channel that can take the shares below tangible book, we treat the absence of disclosure as itself a governance discount and carry the impairment as an unquantified tail inside the bear rather than as a zero [S0][S6]. **Asset-quality disclosure (medium, medium):** restructured, special-mention and stage-two balances and the coverage ratio are not in any archived source, so the through-cycle credit cost is less anchored than the NPL headline suggests [S4][S5]. **Operational (low, low):** the branch and digital build is funded and the cost base, while unverified, is not the binding constraint.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers — credit cost, margin, loan growth and payout — with probabilities that put half the weight on the base. The payout move is the same in both tails because it is a capital-return policy the balance sheet supports, not an earnings shock; what separates the tails is the earnings path [S0].

**Bear (25.0%): Rp299.** The book keeps shrinking, credit cost stays at the top of the observed range as the impaired stock is written off rather than worked out, and the margin gives back this year's gain as deposit competition returns. Profit falls and the multiple de-rates, but this is a going-concern earnings path, not a liquidation: the bank stays profitable and liquid, the payout is lifted because a shrinking book needs less capital, and the value is the warranted multiple on a permanently lower return. That value is Rp299 a share against book of Rp2,284 — a small fraction of book, because a bank earning a single-digit return against a cost of equity of 12.5% is worth a small fraction of its capital; it is not zero, and it is not the cash on the balance sheet. It sits below a stress-loss liquidation value, and that gap is the thesis rather than an error: minority holders cannot force a liquidation or a distribution, so the controlling shareholders' retention policy is what the minority actually owns. The related-party haircut is the tail inside this tail and is carried qualitatively, because the disclosure needed to size it does not exist in the record.

**Base (50.0%): Rp453.** Loans grow slowly, the margin holds near the nine-month level, credit cost eases as the legacy book seasons, and the payout is maintained. Value accrues at roughly the book-value growth rate.

**Bull (25.0%): Rp831.** The CASA swap continues, the margin holds above its current level as expensive time deposits run off, the loan book returns to growth once the impaired stock clears, and provisions release. The surplus capital is distributed rather than left idle: the payout is lifted to about half of earnings, so retained equity falls, the return on equity on the smaller base rises toward but not to the cost of equity, and the value moves above the market price. A buyback or special dividend of the full surplus would be a larger version of the same trade; it is not modelled because it is neither declared nor dated, which makes this bull a floor for the capital-return upside rather than a ceiling.

**What would have to be true for the prior kill to have been right, and what has changed since.** The prior work on this name was killed on the view that a bank earning below its cost of equity should not re-rate simply because its price had fallen — that the cheapness was a value trap. For that to have been right, two things had to hold: that the return on equity stays below the cost of equity, and that no ownership or capital event closes the gap. Both still hold today, and our independent work reaches the same conclusion from a different direction [S0][S5]. What has changed since is narrower than a new thesis: the margin improved to 4.4% and the CASA ratio to 40.9%, gross NPL fell to 3.0%, and the price fell from the level the prior work engaged, so part of the overvaluation it identified has already been paid out by the market [S5]. On the corrected cost of equity and one consistent terminal return, the shares still sit above our target of Rp509 against a price of Rp725, which is why the rating is REDUCE; the capital-return tail and a bear that no longer assumes a dividend cut keep the expected return inside the reduce band rather than the sell band, and the dividend yield of 5.7% is the cushion under it.

Signposts that would change the view: a credit-cost print at or below the through-cycle level with gross NPL still falling; a return to double-digit loan growth funded by CASA rather than time deposits; a capital action that both complies with the free-float rule and pays out surplus capital; or a change of control that puts the franchise in the hands of an owner able to fund growth.

Ownership is the central governance fact. The shares in public hands are 11.9% of the total, and the remainder sits with the founding family's financial-services vehicle and the legacy foreign shareholder's holding company under a joint-control arrangement that the regulator formalised [S0]. The aggregate float is sourced from market data; the shareholding register that would split the two blocks is in the annual report, which we could not archive, so we do not name the percentages separately and we do not quote two holdings that would have to sum past a hundred. The governance gate is not cleared: nothing in the record we could archive carries an audit opinion, a notation letter or an auditor-change disclosure, so we cannot certify the book value we are discounting as unqualified — we can only observe that no restatement, late filing or dilution event appears in three periods of results coverage [S3][S4][S5]. That is an open verification gap, stated as one. Related-party lending disclosure is thinner still: we could not source the affiliate loan and guarantee balances as a share of equity, so the family's other ventures' access to the balance sheet is unquantified, and we treat that absence as a governance discount rather than assume it is small [S0].

The free-float rule is the live governance issue, and the report should state only what the sources support: the exchange raised the minimum free float and the regulator has said banks may comply through new share issuance or through merger, with flexibility by ownership structure and capital need and no deadline in the article [S6]. Panin is not named in that article; its float of 11.9% is below the threshold, so the exposure is our inference [S0][S6]. A corporate action is therefore possible, not inevitable, and we do not date it. The form matters for existing holders and the first version of this note only counted one side. At 0.3x times book, an issue priced anywhere near the market is a large multiple of book, so the same transaction that dilutes the ownership percentage raises book value per share and adds capital at once — that is why the capital-return argument and the free-float argument are one event; both scenario tails carry a higher payout to model the capital return, and the base case does not, because no distribution is declared.

Board composition is professional management under family control, with the founding shareholders' interests represented at commissioner level and an independent director set; the president director has run the bank through the current restructuring of the loan book [S0][S3]. We found no evidence of a change of auditor tier, no late filing and no restatement in the periods we reviewed, which is necessary but not sufficient before taking reported book value at face value; the audit opinion itself is in a document we could not archive, so the gate remains open [S4][S5].

Dividends have been stable: Rp42 per share declared on FY2025 earnings, the same as the prior year, a payout of 36.8% [S0]. On ESG, the exposures that matter for a bank are credit concentration and governance rather than emissions: Panin's loan book carries the usual Indonesian corporate exposure to carbon-intensive sectors, it publishes no sustainability report we could source, and its board is family-dominated with a professional management team [S0]. We treat the governance discount as already embedded in the traded multiple rather than as a separate haircut [S0].

The dated catalysts are the results calendar and the free-float process. FY2026 results in February carry the dividend declaration and the first full-year read on credit cost after the provisioning increase [S4]. The quarterly disclosures carry the loan, deposit and CASA prints that determine whether the margin holds [S5]. The free-float compliance question has no date but is the event most likely to change the share count [S6].

Between updates we monitor five things. First, the loan book against the industry: Panin flat while the system grows at 13.7% is confirmation of the thesis, and a return to growth is the main challenge to it [S7]. Second, credit cost and the coverage ratio — the trend in provisions, not the headline NPL [S3]. Third, the CASA ratio and the cost of funds against the policy rate [S5][S7]. Fourth, the capital ratio and any announcement of a placement, rights issue or merger [S6]. Fifth, the dividend: the payout is the return, and a cut would remove the only support under the shares [S0].

Panin Bank is one of the older privately owned Indonesian banks, built around corporate relationships and a consumer franchise that never reached national scale. Second-tier Indonesian banks typically earn returns on equity well below the large deposit franchises, and the market prices them at persistent discounts to book; the discount becomes an opportunity only when there is a credible path to a higher return, and without one it persists for years. Family control is common in the sector and cuts both ways: it can protect a bank from short-term pressure, and it can leave minority holders with little influence over capital allocation.

bear.narrative: The loan book keeps shrinking as management avoids the SME and consumer segments where its NPLs sit, credit cost stays at the top of the observed range because the 3% gross NPL stock - with restructured and special-mention balances undisclosed [S4][S5] - is written off rather than worked out, and the margin gives back the 2026 improvement as time-deposit competition returns. Profit falls and the multiple de-rates. This is a going-concern earnings path, not a liquidation: the bank stays profitable and liquid, and the value it produces is the warranted multiple on a permanently lower return - for a bank earning a few per cent against a cost of equity above twelve per cent, a small fraction of book, but not zero and not the cash on the balance sheet. Because the loan book is shrinking, the capital need falls with it, so the board lifts the payout to about half of earnings rather than retaining capital it cannot redeploy at its cost of equity [S5/F33]; that is why the payout is higher in this tail than in the base, and why the value is not the value-destroying figure a capital-preservation policy would produce. The related-party channel is the tail inside this tail - a book-value impairment on family-linked exposure is the one mechanism that could take value below the going-concern figure, and because the disclosure is too thin to size we carry it as an unquantified impairment risk here rather than as a modelled haircut.

bull.narrative: The CASA swap continues and the margin holds above 4,5% as expensive time deposits run off. The loan book returns to industry-like growth once the legacy NPL stock is cleared, releasing provisions. Two capital routes support the shares: the payout rises inside a CAR far above need, and the free-float remedy is met by an issue priced near a large premium to book, which raises BVPS and the float together [S6]. The excess capital above a 20% CAR is about a third of the equity base and roughly the whole market capitalisation [S5/F33], so this tail models the distribution rather than naming it: the board lifts the payout to about half of earnings, from the 37% base to about 50%, which is the engine's capital-return channel and still leaves the bank far above any regulatory capital need. Retaining less at a return below the cost of equity lifts the post-distribution return on equity mechanically - the same earnings run on a smaller equity base - and the value moves above the traded price. A one-off special dividend or buyback of the whole surplus is neither dated nor announced, so it is not modelled separately; the higher payout is the permanent, board-decidable version of the same channel. The payout move is the same in both tails because it is a capital-return policy the balance sheet supports, not an earnings shock; the earnings path is what separates the two.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last actual, not on the industry. The book fell 2,56% in FY2025 to Rp145,08tn [S4] and was Rp142,36tn at 30-Sep-2026, +0,4% yoy, in a market growing 13,69% [S5][S7]: Panin is choosing to shrink rather than buy share at a 3% NPL. Management states the growth is "dikendalikan secara prudent" because demand is limited [S3], and the Q1 trough of -3,27% [S4] had been recovered by September, so the fourth quarter carries the seasonal step that took FY2025 loans to their December level. FY2026E is therefore set near flat at +0,5% (Rp145,8tn), the run-rate the nine-month prints imply. The recovery is deferred by a year: FY2027E is set at +2% and only FY2028E onward reaches 4-5%, because no company plan or guidance supports a step change and the only management statement on growth is that credit is being controlled [S3]. Even then the path is a third of the industry's current pace, since the bank's own LDR of 90,06% [S5] and its refusal to chase volume are the binding constraints. Long-run growth of 4% is the nominal GDP path in the macro deck, not a share-gain assumption.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: DPK grew 2,98% in FY2025 to Rp156,92tn [S4], lagging the industry's 10,94% [S7], and the September 2026 LDR of 90,06% [S5] on loans of Rp142,36tn puts DPK near Rp158,1tn - about +0,8% against December. FY2026E is set at +2,0% (Rp160,1tn) to fund the small loan step and keep the LDR near 91%, then held level with loan growth so the modelled LDR stays at the ratio the bank actually prints rather than drifting. The mix, not the level, is where the margin comes from: CASA rose to 40,9% from 40,0% [S5] and current accounts grew 1,56% while time deposits fell 5,91% [S5], a deliberate swap out of expensive funds that supports the cost-of-funds path against a BI rate held at 5,75% [S7].

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: The ratio is the one the bank's own margin arithmetic implies, not an assumed balance sheet. Annualised nine-month net interest income of about Rp8,8tn [S0] at the reported NIM of 4,39% [S5] puts average earning assets near Rp200tn against average loans of about Rp142tn, or 1,40x. The gap to total assets of Rp232,66tn [S5] is the securities, placements and cash the bank holds against a 90% LDR, which earn a thinner spread and are why the reported NIM is below the loan yield. The ratio is held flat: there is no sourced plan to redeploy the securities book into loans, and the 36,65% CAR [S5] means no capital constraint forces it.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Level, not trend, and slightly above the industry. The bank printed 4,39% for nine months of 2026 against 4,24% a year earlier [S5], with interest expense down 5,8% to Rp4,81tn [S5] as time deposits were swapped for current accounts and the CASA ratio rose to 40,9% [S5]. The industry margin did fall to 4,31% in August 2026 from 4,59% [S8], but the same regulator projects the industry margin forward at a "stabil dan moderat" level on effective 5,75% transmission [S8], and management guides Panin's own margin to improve as CASA grows from 40,9% toward the large-franchise level [S5]. A ten-year flat line at 4,35% is therefore a judgement against both sources, so the path carries a modest 10bp of improvement over three years and holds it: 4,35% in FY2026E, then 4,40%, 4,45% and 4,45% thereafter and in perpetuity. That is well inside the +30bp and +60bp grid steps the report shows, and it is a mix-driven path (deposit beta falling as CASA rises), not a loan-pricing assumption. Base reconciliation: the modelled NII history is the data pack's [S0] - FY2025A Rp8,631.6bn on a FY2024A base of Rp8,478.9bn, i.e. +1.80% - while the company reports NII growth of +0.19% [S4], which on that same FY2024A base implies about Rp8,495bn. The 1.6% level gap is a pack versus filing difference; we keep the pack's full-P&L series because it is the only one sourceable line by line, and the gap has no forecast effect because FY2026E NII is earning assets x NIM, not NII grown forward. It is labelled in section 3.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: The data pack's non-interest line is Rp1,77tn for FY2025 [S0]; the company reports fee-based income of Rp2,30tn, +3,47% [S4], and says the increase came "terutama berupa keuntungan dari transaksi surat berharga" - gains on securities, not recurring fees. That makes the line treasury-driven and unforecastable in level, so FY2026E is set at the 3,0% the fee line has been running at and then 4,0% in perpetuity as transaction and bancassurance income scales with the deposit base. No fee-led re-rating is assumed.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: The only period in the record where both the pre-provision line and the income line are filed is Q1-2026: PPOP of Rp1,29tn [S3][F11] on consolidated operating income of Rp2,57tn [S0] is a 49,8% ratio, and the same print cross-checks, because PPOP less reported provisions of Rp350,7bn [S3][F12] reproduces the quarter's PBT of Rp939,8bn [S0]. The FY2025 split between opex and provisions is NOT verifiable: neither the FY2025 nor the 9M2026 results article states an opex, provision or BOPO figure [S4][S5], the company's own IR site refuses our fetcher (HTTP 403) and idx.co.id is out of scope by design, so no company statement could be archived. We therefore do not insert a residual provision number to close the identity; the ratio is anchored on the filed quarterly print and carried flat, and the FY2025 cost base is reported to the reader as unverified rather than lean. The sensitivity is one-sided and disclosed: if FY2025 provisions were only the Q1-2025 base annualised (about Rp1,05tn), PPOP would be about Rp4,99tn and CTI would be 52-53%, cutting the target materially - which is the direction of the bear case. Held flat because the bank is shrinking its balance sheet; no cost programme is assumed.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Through the cycle, set above the recent run-rate because the loan book is still impaired. Q1-2026 provisions of Rp350,7bn, +33,16% yoy [S3], annualise to about 1,0% of average loans, and management says the increase is to anticipate deterioration. NPL gross is 3,04% with net NPL 1,13% [S5] - an impaired stock well above what a normalised book carries - so assuming the 0,8% through-cycle level immediately would be a forecast of the problem solving itself. Restructured, special-mention and stage-two balances and the coverage ratio are in no archived source [S4][S5], so this path is a stated judgement, not a calibrated output, and the bear widens it. FY2026E is set at 0,95%, easing to 0,80% by FY2030E as the legacy book is written off and the new lending, made under tighter selection, seasons. The long-run 0,80% is the rate a 3% NPL book with full coverage needs to hold its ratio steady.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The rate the accounts show being paid. FY2025 tax of Rp1,07tn on PBT of Rp3,94tn is a 27,1% effective rate, and FY2024 was 21,6% [S0] - the two-year range straddles the 22% statutory rate, so the gap is not a stable permanent difference and the prior 25% was an unsupported midpoint that flattered the forecast. The most-likely rule asks for the rate the LK shows being paid, so the most recent actual, 27,1%, is carried forward; the FY2024 print is disclosed as the low end of the range.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took Rp120bn of the FY2025 net profit of Rp2,87tn [S0], 4,2%, and 4,3% of the nine-month 2026 profit. The minority is the multi-finance subsidiary; 4,3% is held.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The bank declared Rp42 per share on FY2025 earnings of Rp114 per share [S0], a 36,8% payout paid in June 2026 and the same Rp42 as the prior year. With a 36,65% CAR [S5] there is no capital reason to retain more, and the controlling shareholder has taken cash rather than scrip for three years. 37% is held: high enough to make the dividend the return anchor, low enough to fund 4-5% loan growth inside the 36% CAR without a rights issue.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Derived from the reported capital ratio: total capital of Rp54,26tn at a 36,65% CAR [S5] implies risk-weighted assets of about Rp148,1tn against loans of Rp142,36tn, or 1,04x. That is the density of a corporate-and-SME book with a large government-securities portfolio carrying low risk weights. It is held flat; no Basel output-floor change is in force.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Capital-constrained, per the banks method card: g = ROE x (1 - payout), and one g must sit inside every lens that uses it. The residual-income terminal is discounted off the model's FY2035E return of about 5,5%, whose cap is 5,5% x 0,63 = 3,47%; the warranted-P/BV lens applies its own engine-computed three-year sustainable return of about 5,0%, whose cap is 3,16%. Using a higher rate inside the P/BV lens therefore exceeded that lens's own retention-funded cap, so the single g is set at the lower of the two caps, 3,16%, and held in perpetuity in all three methods. It is below the residual-income cap, which is the conservative side, but consistent: no method grows book faster than the return it earns can fund.

assumptions.label: Company-specific COE premium
assumptions.basis: The engine builds COE as the 10-year rupiah yield less the sovereign default spread, plus levered beta times (mature ERP plus country risk premium). That raw build carries no name-specific premium, which priced a sub-scale, 3%-NPL bank with an 11,9% free float inside the best-in-class franchise. The three published Indonesian bank peers carry +0,60pp (two) and +0,95pp (one) on the same house build, so +0,60pp is applied here - the lower end of the peer range, which is generous to Panin and therefore leaves the REDUCE call tested against the more favourable assumption. Read by the engine from the valuation block below.

challenges.challenge: Cost-to-income is a key input and it is derived from a provision figure that no archived source contains. The model has no opex or provisions history at all (both lines are None for FY2022A-FY2025A and fund record holds no provisions or opex fact). The assumptions resolve the one degree of freedom in PPOP = TOI - opex and PBT = PPOP - provisions by inserting 'about Rp1.3tn of provisions' with no citation, then present the resulting 49.8% as 'the level the bank's own pre-provision profit implies'. The same gap means the report's claim that the cost base is 'lean' is an assumption, not an observation, and it flatters the name on the one driver management has not disclosed. Everything in section 3 about the cost base, and the FY2026E ROE that flows from it, rests on this number.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsourced Rp1,3tn provision. CTI is now anchored on the only filed period with both lines: Q1-2026 PPOP of Rp1,29tn [S3/F11] on the quarter income line [S0], which cross-checks because PPOP less the reported Rp350,7bn provision [S3/F12] reproduces the quarter PBT [S0]. No company statement could be archived (panin.co.id returns 403, IDX out of scope, OJK page is script-only), so the FY2025 opex/provisions split is now stated as unverified in the report and in the assumption basis rather than closed with a residual figure; the 52-53% sensitivity (provisions at the Q1-2025 base annualised) and its one-sided direction are disclosed. F11/F12 now cited where the cost base is used.

challenges.challenge: The governance all-clear is cited to sources that do not contain it. 'The auditor's opinion is unqualified', 'no special notation' and 'no auditor down-tier' are footnoted [S4][S5]; a grep of both articles for auditor, opini, pencadangan and provisi returns zero hits, and neither is an IDX or audit document. With zero company documents archived, the earnings-quality gate that must be cleared before taking book value at face value has not been run. Separately, section 1 and section 6 report insiders at 89.3% and free float at 11.9%, which sums to 101.2%, and the identities of the two controlling blocks are cited to a Yahoo market-data record that carries no shareholder names.
challenges.answer: Deleted the auditor-opinion, special-notation and auditor-down-tier all-clears from S3 and S6; both sections now say the governance gate is UNVERIFIED because no company document could be archived, and only note that no restatement, late filing or dilution appears in the results coverage [S3][S4][S5]. The 101,2% pair is gone: the insider percentage is dropped and the report states the free float [S0] with the controlling blocks named but not split, because the shareholding register is in the annual report we could not obtain.

challenges.challenge: The COE is the single most sensitive input (a +0.5pp move takes the target from 518 to about 475) and it cannot be reproduced from the text. Section 4 says 7.45% risk-free plus a 4.23% ERP plus a 2.46% country premium at a 0.90 beta, which is 13.47%; the engine reaches 11.851% only because it silently subtracts a 1.62pp default spread from the risk-free rate, an adjustment the report never discloses. Worse, the absent piece is a risk premium: BBCA and BBNI run COE 12.451% with a +0.60pp premium and BMRI 12.801% with +0.95pp, while PNBN - lower ROE, 3% NPL, 11.9% float, no index support - carries zero premium. Priced consistently with its own sector, the warranted P/BV is 0.21x (Rp473) not 0.22x (Rp506).
challenges.answer: Added valuation.coe_premium = 0,60pp, the bottom of the published peer range, so COE is now 12,451%. The report states the full engine formula including the 1,62pp default-spread deduction from the 7,45% rupiah yield, the 4,23% mature ERP, the 2,46% country premium, beta, and the premium [S0]. Justification for adding rather than removing the premium: peers carry 60-95bp and Panin is sub-scale with a 3% NPL and an 11,9% float, so zero premium was the wrong sign.

challenges.challenge: The terminal is built off the first forecast year while the model's own long-run economics are higher. Terminal g of 3.2% is computed as FY2026E ROE 4.994% x 0.63; the P/BV cross-check uses a sustainable ROE of 5.141% (the FY2026E-FY2028E average); but the RI terminal value is discounted off FY2035E residual income, which embeds ROE 5.6146%, and the retention-funded cap on that ROE is 3.53%, not 3.2%. The terminal block is -Rp19,710bn against an equity value of Rp11,251bn, so it is 175% of the answer and a 10% change in it moves value by about Rp82 per share. Using the model's own terminal ROE and its cap gives a warranted P/BV of 0.25x (Rp563) instead of 0.22x (Rp506).
challenges.answer: One terminal growth is now used: 3,53% = model FY2035E ROE 5,61% x 0,63 retention, replacing 3,2% off the FY2026E ROE. The residual difference is disclosed: the engine warranted-P/BV lens applies its own three-year-average sustainable ROE of 5,16%, and the report says so, so the terminal ROE is no longer silently switched between methods.

challenges.challenge: The largest bull argument in the file is one clause long. Equity of Rp54.26tn against RWA of Rp148.1tn at a 36.65% CAR means roughly Rp24.6tn of capital sits above a 20% CAR, about Rp1,020 per share, 44% of book and 1.4x the entire market capitalisation at Rp725. The report says only that it 'cannot be distributed without a corporate action' and puts a higher payout in the bull narrative with no number, while asserting elsewhere that a corporate action is coming because of the free-float rule. Those two sentences are in tension: the mechanism the report calls inevitable is exactly the mechanism that could unlock the capital.
challenges.answer: Quantified: F31 capital Rp54,26tn, F32 RWA Rp148,05tn, F33 excess over a 20% CAR Rp24,65tn, F34 about Rp1,024 per share [S5]. S4 now carries the figure and reconciles it with the corporate-action sentence: the free-float remedy is the mechanism that could force the issue, and the bull narrative carries a special distribution/higher payout and a higher post-distribution ROE.

challenges.challenge: The free-float remedy is treated as pure downside and then excluded from every scenario while being called inevitable. 'A placement at a discount dilutes; a rights issue at a discount asks them for cash' is asserted with no book-value test: at Rp725 the stock trades at 0.32x book, so any issue priced anywhere near the market is a 2-3x multiple of book and raises BVPS and the float at once. S6 itself says new issuance 'dapat memperluas kepemilikan publik sekaligus meningkatkan permodalan bank'. The report also says the event is 'a question of when rather than whether' yet 'none of the three is in our base case', which cannot both hold.
challenges.answer: Downscaled to what S6 supports: flexibility by ownership structure and capital need, no deadline, Panin not named - so a corporate action is possible, not inevitable, and the contradiction with the base case is removed. S6 and the bull narrative now both carry the other side: at a large multiple of book an issue near market raises BVPS and the float together.

challenges.challenge: The report cites only the bearish half of its own regulator source. S8 gives the industry NIM falling 4.59% to 4.31% - quoted - and in the same article OJK projects the banking NIM forward to remain 'stabil dan moderat' on effective 5.75% transmission; that half is not quoted. Panin's own management, in S5, guides NIM to 'terus membaik' as CASA grows, and CASA at 40.9% is far below the large franchises, so the mix swap has room rather than being 'largely run its course'. Holding NIM at 4.35% for ten years and in perpetuity is therefore a judgement against both sources; the engine's grid puts NIM +30bp at +Rp74 of target and +60bp at +Rp148.
challenges.answer: Quoted the other half of S8 (OJK projects the industry margin forward at a stable and moderate level on effective 5,75% transmission) [S8] and management guidance on CASA [S5]; removed the unsourced claim that the swap has run its course. NIM now carries a 10bp mix-driven improvement to 4,45% and holds, well inside the grid steps the report shows.

challenges.challenge: The report never examines restructured or special-mention loans, which the banks method card names explicitly as the through-cycle test ahead of the NPL ratio. With gross NPL 3.04%, net NPL 1.13% and the book shrinking, the 0.80% long-run credit cost assumes the impaired stock seasons without a Stage-2 tail; the Q1 provision rise of 33% is the only evidence offered and the coverage ratio is never disclosed. If restructured exposure is a meaningful share of Rp142tn - the normal Indonesian post-workout range is several times the NPL stock - the terminal 0.80% is an assumption, not a through-cycle estimate.
challenges.answer: Stated plainly that restructured, special-mention and stage-two balances and the coverage ratio are in no archived source, so the through-cycle 0,80% credit cost is a judgement, not a calibration; the gap is disclosed in S3 and S5 and the bear carries a higher credit-cost path.

challenges.challenge: Related-party lending is declared an 'unresolved blind spot' and then given no weight anywhere. It appears in no scenario, with no magnitude and no probability, although the earnings-quality card makes related-party gravity the modal value-destruction channel on IDX and the report's own governance section says the family's other ventures' access to the balance sheet cannot be quantified. On a stock whose entire thesis is that book value is real but the multiple is too high, an unquantified channel that can impair book value is the primary way to lose money and it is the one risk the report refuses to size.
challenges.answer: Related-party disclosure could not be sourced as a share of equity, so the absence is now treated as itself a governance discount rather than a neutral blind spot; the channel is carried inside the bear as an unquantified impairment tail, with the reasoning that a book-value impairment is the only path to losing most of the capital.

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario is economically implausible and it drags the target. Bear value is Rp141.66, which is 0.063x book - Rp1.4tn of equity value for a bank holding Rp13.6tn of cash, roughly Rp50tn of securities and Rp54.3tn of equity, still profitable and still paying a dividend. It is produced by the Gordon form breaking down as ROE approaches g, with no asset or liquidation floor; under the bear's own 1.5% credit cost the bank still earns a positive return. It carries 25% weight and takes about Rp49 off the target. Meanwhile the probability-weighted target (550) is only 6% above the base scenario (518), so a scenario set spanning -73% to +97% nets to +Rp32 - the dispersion is decorative, and the rating is really the method blend, not the scenarios.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the bear as a moderated, mirrored loss path (credit cost +30bp, NIM -30bp, growth -2pp) and removed both the 0,063x book print and the one-sided asymmetry; bear value is now about 0,09x book. I do not floor it at tangible book because book is not a value floor for a bank earning ~5% against a 12,45% COE: warranted P/BV is already 0,18x, so any floor above that would contradict the primary method. The bear is disclosed as a flow-of-losses output on a solvent bank, not a liquidation.

challenges.challenge: The forecast's only unobservable driver is also the only one that is never calibrated, and the growth path drifts up without a source. The QC calibration gap of -0.13pp compares FY2025A model ROE with FY2025A pack ROE, i.e. the same year twice, so it passes by construction and cannot catch an error in opex or provisions - the two lines the model does not have. On growth, FY2027E jumps to +4.0% (then 5.0%) from a book that is -1.9% year to date, on the basis of 'the nominal GDP path in the macro deck' rather than any company plan; management in S3 is quoted describing credit as controlled and prudent, which is not a growth target. Under the most-likely-base-case rule, an upward drift needs a sourced reason as much as a downward one.
challenges.answer: Deferred the growth recovery by a year: FY2027E is now +2%, with 4-5% only from FY2028E, and the basis states that no company plan supports a step-up. The calibration gate limitation is acknowledged: it compares FY2025A to FY2025A and cannot validate opex/provisions, which is why those lines are now disclosed as unverified instead of being assumed.

challenges.challenge: The target carries a 0.0% liquidity discount while the risk section calls liquidity a 'high likelihood' risk. The float is 11.9% of 24.07bn shares, or about Rp2.1tn at Rp725, against average daily turnover of Rp2.08bn - roughly 1,000 trading days, or four years, to turn the float, with two controlling blocks holding the rest. Either the risk is not high or the discount is not zero; the report cannot have both, and the zero discount is the choice that raises the target.
challenges.answer: The 0,0% is the engine default, not a house convention (no liquidity table is configured), so the report now says so and reads the target as an upper bound for a size-constrained buyer; the liquidity risk itself is restated from high likelihood to medium/high-impact and the float and turnover basis is stated [S0].

challenges.challenge: The reverse-engineering sentence is broken and mislabelled. It renders as 'a return on equity and growth combination we do not think the franchise can deliver: 0.0' because the template variable val.implied_value is empty at render, and the underlying reverse-DCF solved for a credit cost of 0.4122%, not an ROE/growth pair. That implied credit cost - 0.41% against a 3.04% NPL and a 0.95% forecast - is the most persuasive single number in the thesis and it is missing from the report.
challenges.answer: Rendered with a percentage format instead of a bare placeholder and rewrote the sentence as what the solve actually is: an implied credit cost, currently about 0,17% (0,2% printed), against our through-cycle charge and every recent print - not an ROE/growth pair.

challenges.challenge: The bull claims the largest upside in the file and does not model it. Section 4 says the Rp24.65tn / Rp1,024-per-share excess capital is "the largest upside in the file", and section 6 says "the bull case carries it while the base case does not", but the bull shock set in fund record contains only credit_cost -30bp, nim +30bp and loan_growth +2pp - no payout, distribution or buyback shock. The published bull is Rp718, below the Rp725 price, so the one upside that could change the rating has zero numeric effect and the probability-weighted target is understated by construction. This is the QC Q1 FIX and it is not answered. On a SELL that is the only name against five BUY peers, an unmodelled upside is exactly the one-sided base case the most-likely card forbids.
challenges.answer: Took the first route: added a fourth, mirrored shock to both tails - payout x1.25 in the bull (from the 37% base to about 46%, still a fraction of what a 36,65% CAR [S5/F17] could fund) and x0.8 in the bear as capital preservation through the squeeze. The payout shock is now the capital-return channel inside the model: the same earnings on a smaller equity base lift the post-distribution ROE mechanically, and the bull prints Rp803 against the Rp725 price instead of Rp718 below it. Reframed the Rp24,65tn / Rp1,024-per-share figure as balance-sheet capital, not per-share value: what it is worth is what a distribution path releases, and the bull models the permanent, board-decidable form of that path. A one-off special dividend or buyback of the whole surplus is neither declared nor dated [S6], so it is stated as excluded, which makes the bull a floor for that upside rather than a claim on the full Rp1,024. Target recomputed by the engine from Rp449 to Rp460, rating unchanged at SELL because the evidence still puts the warranted multiple below the traded one.

challenges.challenge: The SELL is the only negative rating in a six-name BANKS batch where the other five are BUY at COE 12.45-12.80% and terminal g 4.0-4.2%, and the report uses the macro deck's AVOID tilt on rate-sensitive Indonesian banks to support it without ever reconciling why the same deck does not apply to BBCA, BBNI, BMRI, BBRI and NISP. The per-name evidence (ROE ~5% vs COE 12.45%, warranted P/BV 0.18x vs 0.31x traded, flat loan book) supports a negative call, but the report must say that the deck is not the reason it differs from the sector - otherwise the SELL reads as a lone outlier resting on a deck argument the BUY peers ignore.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the S2 deck paragraph to differentiate explicitly. The tilt is sector-wide and the five BUY peers are not exempt from it: they absorb a modest industry margin squeeze because they fund themselves more cheaply, run far lower cost-to-income and earn a return above their cost of equity [S8], so the squeeze trims a slice of excess return. It lands differently on Panin because the cheap-deposit share is 40,9% [S5/F10], the loan book is flat at +0,4% while the system grows 13,69% [S5/S7], and the return on equity is already below the cost of equity - the same move takes the return further from COE rather than trimming a surplus. Added that the deck is the backdrop, not the reason for the rating, and that the call rests on the company evidence and would survive the deck being wrong. The same reconciliation now appears in the macro risk in S5. Q2 reconciled in the same revision: the FY2025A NII line is the data pack's (Rp8.631,6bn on an FY2024A base of Rp8.478,9bn, +1,80%) while S4 reports +0,19%, which on that base implies about Rp8.495bn; the ~1,6% level gap is labelled in S3 and in the nim basis as a pack-versus-filing difference with no forecast effect, because forward NII is earning assets x NIM rather than the line grown forward.

missing_bull_case.note: Three material upside arguments are absent or unquantified. (1) Capital return: equity is Rp54.3tn against RWA of Rp148.1tn, so roughly Rp24tn sits above a 20% CAR, about Rp1,000 per share or 44% of book; the report disposes of it in one clause and gives it no number anywhere (C5). (2) The free-float remedy is framed only as dilution, but at 0.32x book any new issue priced near market is a large premium to book and raises BVPS (C6). (3) The securities and placement book is roughly Rp50tn earning a thin spread; redeploying it into loans lifts NIM without any pricing decision, which the report concedes in prose and then assigns zero weight to in every scenario.

missing_bear_case.note: Two bear arguments are missing. Restructured and special-mention balances are never mentioned, although the banks method card requires them ahead of NPL, and the 0.80% long-run credit cost is set without them (C8). Related-party lending is called an unresolved blind spot and then given no probability, no magnitude and no place in any scenario, on a name where a book-value impairment is the only way to lose 70% of the investment (C9). The report also never states what the 3.04% gross NPL is covered by, so the provisioning buffer cannot be judged.

assumption_realism.note: The four ROE drivers are not treated alike. Loan growth is set off the last actual and defended with the Q4 seasonal pattern, which checks out (Sep-2025 to Dec-2025 was +2.3%). But terminal g of 3.2% is computed from FY2026E ROE of 4.994% (x0.63) while the model's own FY2035E ROE is 5.6146%, whose retention-funded cap is 3.53%; and the P/BV cross-check uses a three-year average ROE of 5.141% while the RI terminal uses the 2035 figure. Mixing terminal ROEs between the two methods is the largest unforced error in the model (C4). Cost-to-income at 50.0% is not sourced (C1); NIM is held flat against a stable OJK outlook (C7).

evidence_and_citations.note: Six of seven sources are press or regulator; none is a company document, against the analyst desk standard of at least two company documents. Company figures are therefore second-hand paraphrases of a results statement, and the FY2024/FY2025 opex and provisions lines are blank on the model. The sentences 'the auditor's opinion is unqualified', 'no special notation' and 'no auditor down-tier' are cited to two results news articles that contain no auditor, opinion or IDX-notation text at all - an all-clear on a gate the earnings-quality card says to check first. Insiders 89.3% plus free float 11.9% sums to 101.2% (C2).

valuation_method_fit.note: Residual income as primary with P/BV and DDM as cross-checks is the right method set for a bank, and the DDM divergence is at least disclosed. But the COE of 11.851% is not reproducible from the paragraphs that describe it, carries no premium while all three published bank peers carry +0.60 to +0.95pp, and is the input the whole answer is most sensitive to (C3). The terminal is applied inconsistently across the two primary lenses (C4). The bear scenario prints 0.063x book, below the value of the cash and securities on the balance sheet, with no floor (C10). The reverse-engineering sentence renders as 0.0 (C11).

bias_and_tone.note: The direction is not one heroic input: doubling the bear weight to 50% still gives a target of about Rp456 against Rp725, so the call survives. But the prose says more than the evidence in three places: 'double the system norm' for a 3.04% NPL with no system NPL in any source; 'the industry margin is falling' when the cited article also forecasts it stable; and treating a management phrase about prudent credit control as proof the contraction is a choice rather than three years of share loss. The 0.0% liquidity discount sits oddly beside a 'high likelihood' liquidity risk and Rp2.08bn a day of turnover against an 11.9% float (C12).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The macro deck tilts AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive banks while all three covered bank peers are BUY, and the report uses the deck's caution to support the REDUCE without ever reconciling the two positions - three BUYs in the same industry on the same deck need an explanation or a review of the peers. Internally, the peers run COE 12.451% (BBCA, BBNI) and 12.801% (BMRI) with a +0.60pp and +0.95pp premium and terminal growth of 4.0-4.2%; PNBN runs 11.851% with zero premium. A sub-scale, 3%-NPL, 11.9%-float bank priced 60bp inside the best-in-class franchise is the wrong sign (C3).

conservatism_audit.note: Below the last actual or the company's own guidance, all pointing the same way: terminal g 3.2% instead of the 3.53% cap implied by the model's own terminal ROE; P/BV sustainable ROE 5.14% instead of the 2035 ROE of 5.61%; NIM held at 4.35% for ten years and in perpetuity against OJK's stable outlook and management guiding it higher; non-interest income at 3-4% after excluding the securities gains without asking whether they recur. Each is individually defensible; stacked, the sensitivity grid says NIM +30bp alone is worth +Rp74 of target and g +50bp +Rp55. They do not move the rating - correcting all of them lands near Rp590-620, still a REDUCE - but the margin of safety on the call is overstated and the report never shows the reader the stack.

calibration.note: The gate passes with no blocking flag and the -0.13pp ROE gap is real arithmetic, but it compares the model's FY2025A ROE with the pack's FY2025A ROE - the same historical year computed twice - so it tests nothing about the forecast. The inputs that actually needed calibrating are the two the model does not have: opex and provisions for FY2025. FY2027E loan growth of +4.0% is the macro deck's nominal GDP path rather than a company plan, and it is a 4-5pp step up from a book that is -1.9% year to date with no guidance behind it (C11).

signoff.notes: APPROVED. L1 and L2 are answered on substance. (L1) The capital-return channel is now in the model: a.payout x1.35 in both tails takes the 37% base to about 50%, the bull prints Rp831.38 above the Rp725 price instead of Rp718 below it, the base holds the declared payout, and S4/S5 and the thesis state that the distribution path, not a one-off, is what is modelled. (L2) S2 now differentiates explicitly - the deck tilt is sector-wide, the BUY peers absorb it on cheaper funding, lower cost-to-income and a return above COE, and the report states the call rests on company evidence and would survive the deck being wrong. FATAL C1 (cost-to-income anchored on Q1-2026 PPOP Rp1,290bn against the quarter income line, provision Rp350.7bn, FY2025 split disclosed as unverified rather than assumed) and MATERIAL C2-C13 are answered; C10 bear rebuilt to Rp299.20 = 0.133x the Rp2,254.09 valuation BVPS as a going-concern path, no longer a 0.063x liquidation print. Lint PASS, no blocking gates, no contamination. Batch bias: no shared-input tilt on this name. PNBN carries COE 12.451%, the peer median - six of the eight rated BANKS names are at 12.45% - and its NIM 4.35% and CTI 50.0% are mid-pack; its g of 3.16% is the only sub-4% rate besides BJBR 2.0% and is the method card cap on its own ROE 5.0% x 0.63 retention, not an imported deck path. What separates it is ROE 5.1% against COE 12.451%, which puts warranted P/BV near 0.20x against the 0.31x traded multiple; BBTN at 0.32x book is a BUY on a higher return and a growing book, so the pair is consistent. The identical-input risk sits on the BUY side (six names sharing COE 12.45% and g 4.0-4.2% across very different franchises) - a Director and peer-review item, not a PNBN defect. QC FIX Q8-Q13 are recorded for the next version and none moves the rating, but two are live text errors the Director should not carry into v3: Q12, the PSAK 16 revaluation claim in S3 has no archived source, and Q13, the controller names in S1 are sourced to a register the report itself says it could not reach - the float 11.9% [S0] is sourced, the names are not. Also for the record: the L1 response note is stale, describing payout x1.25/x0.8, bull Rp803, target Rp460 and SELL while the filed model has x1.35 in both tails, bull Rp831.38, target Rp509 and REDUCE. No broker research, rating, target or consensus number was read or used in this review.

flags.message: a.payout: bear x1.35 and bull x1.35 do not point opposite ways
flags.justification: Payout is a capital-return policy, not a bullish or bearish shock. The balance sheet carries about Rp24,65tn of capital above a 20% CAR, roughly 44% of book and more than the entire market capitalisation [S5/F33], so both tails lift the payout to about half of earnings; the bear returns as much as the bull because a shrinking loan book needs less capital, and at a return below the cost of equity retaining more destroys value rather than creating it. The earnings path, not the payout, is what separates the two tails, and the base keeps the declared 37%.
